Let’s unpack this: when scientists want to estimate ETo across a large region—like a country or continent—they often don’t have weather stations everywhere. So they need to *interpolate*, which means estimating values at locations where no measurements were taken, based on data from nearby stations. One powerful method for doing this is called *spline interpolation*. Think of it like drawing a smooth curve through scattered data points—imagine connecting dots on a map with a flexible ruler that bends just enough to pass through each point without sharp turns. This method is especially useful when the variable being estimated, like temperature, changes gradually with geography.

But here’s a key insight: temperature, humidity, and wind don’t just change randomly—they’re strongly influenced by elevation. As you go higher in altitude, the air gets cooler. So if you ignore elevation when interpolating temperature, your estimates could be way off, especially in mountainous areas. That’s why the authors used a *spline model with dependency on elevation*—they built elevation right into the interpolation process. This means the model doesn’t just look at how close two stations are on a map, but also how different they are in height. This leads to much more accurate temperature estimates, which in turn improves ETo calculations.
Mardikis et al. (2005) also show that the performance of interpolation of ETo estimation highly improved when elevation is incorporated.

This isn’t just a minor tweak—it’s a game-changer. When elevation is ignored, interpolation might assume that a valley and a nearby mountain peak have similar temperatures, which is clearly wrong. By including elevation as a controlling factor, the model can predict that higher locations will be cooler, leading to lower ETo (since cooler air holds less moisture and evaporates less water). This makes the resulting ETo maps far more realistic, especially in regions with complex terrain.
Similarly, Raziei and Pereira (2013b) estimated ETo for Iran using climate variables interpolated to regular grid points prior to estimating ETo with PM method.

Let’s break this down. First, they took scattered weather station data and used interpolation (likely elevation-aware) to fill in the gaps across Iran, creating a uniform grid of climate data—like turning a patchy quilt into a smooth, continuous fabric. Then, at each grid point, they applied the Penman-Monteith (PM) method, which is the gold standard for calculating ETo. The PM method combines several factors—solar radiation, temperature, humidity, and wind speed—to estimate how much water would evaporate from a well-watered grass surface. By doing this across a grid, they created a complete spatial map of ETo for the entire country.
Observation-based gridded datasets could be used as an alternative source of data for ETo computation (Haslinger and Bartsch 2016; Raziei and Pereira 2013b; Tomas-Burguera et al. 2018).

These are pre-made grids of climate data created by organizations that collect and process weather observations from thousands of stations worldwide. Instead of starting from scratch, researchers can download these ready-to-use datasets and plug them directly into the PM equation. It’s like buying a pre-cut puzzle instead of carving each piece by hand—it saves time and effort.

However, such datasets may not provide all the needed data at global scale or may not reasonably represent the real amplitude and time variation of variables in areas where few stations have been used for gridding.

This is a critical limitation. Imagine trying to draw a detailed portrait of a person using only three dots for the entire face—you might get the rough outline, but the fine details will be missing or distorted. Similarly, in regions with very few weather stations (like remote deserts or mountain ranges), the gridded data might smooth out important variations. For example, a sudden drop in temperature at night or a sharp spike in wind speed during a storm might be averaged out, making the data look calmer and more stable than reality.

For example, the daily gridded dataset E-OBS for land areas of Europe (Haylock et al. 2008) provides all the variables necessary for ETo computation but their accuracy in a given area is conditioned to the number of stations used for gridding.

E-OBS is a high-quality dataset for Europe, but its strength depends entirely on data density. In countries like Germany or France, where there are many weather stations, E-OBS is very reliable. But in more remote parts of Eastern Europe or mountainous regions like the Balkans, where stations are sparse, the interpolated values are more uncertain. So while E-OBS gives a complete picture, the *trustworthiness* of that picture varies from place to place.

Likewise, remote sensing data that measure some required variables for ETo estimation, including surface albedo and surface radiation, could be used as proxy data for studying evapotranspiration at large spatial scales (Sheffield et al. 2006).

Remote sensing—data collected from satellites—offers a powerful alternative. Satellites can "see" the Earth’s surface continuously, capturing information like how much sunlight is reflected (albedo) or how much energy is emitted as heat (surface radiation). These are key inputs for ETo models. While satellites may not measure humidity or wind speed directly, they can estimate radiation variables with high spatial detail, filling gaps where ground stations are missing. This makes remote sensing ideal for monitoring evapotranspiration across continents or even the entire globe.

The global atmospheric reanalysis datasets such as the National Centers for Environmental Prediction–National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCEP/NCAR, Kalnay et al. 1996; Kistler et al. 2001), the 15- and 40-yr European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF ERA-15 and ERA-40, Gibson et al. 1997), Era-Interim and Era5 (Hans et al. 2019; Hans et al. 2018), the NCEP–Department of Energy (DOE, Kanamitsu et al. 2002), and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Data Assimilation Office (NASA DAO, Schubert et al. 1993) can provide the required variables for ETo estimation at high temporal resolution.

Reanalysis datasets are like weather time machines. They combine historical observations (from stations, satellites, balloons, etc.) with modern weather models to reconstruct past atmospheric conditions in a consistent way. Unlike raw observations, which can be patchy and inconsistent over time, reanalysis provides a complete, gap-free record of variables like temperature, humidity, wind, and radiation—hour by hour, day by day, for decades.

These reanalysis products are constructed using “frozen” versions of numerical weather prediction and assimilation systems. Meaning that they ingest a variety of atmospheric and sea surface observations to provide long-term atmospheric and land surface variables while being temporally and spatially continuous, self-consistent, and readily available.

The term “frozen” here means that the model version used to generate the dataset is fixed—scientists don’t keep updating the model as new versions come out. This is crucial because it ensures consistency over time. If the model changed every few years, differences in the output might reflect model improvements rather than real climate changes. By using a fixed model, reanalysis datasets allow researchers to study long-term trends with confidence.
However, their coarse spatial resolution could be considered a shortcoming (Sheffield et al. 2006).

Most global reanalysis datasets have grid cells that are tens or even hundreds of kilometers wide. That’s fine for studying large-scale weather patterns, but problematic for local applications. For instance, a single grid cell might cover both a hot desert and a cool mountain range, and the model would report an average value—missing the extreme differences within the cell. This is like describing the temperature of an entire city with one number, ignoring the fact that downtown is hotter than the suburbs.

Despite observed biases in some reanalysis products (Berg et al. 2003; Ngo-Duc et al. 2005; Sheffield et al. 2004), they have already been successfully used by many authors for modeling land surface water and energy balances (Maurer et al. 2001, 2002; Roads and Betts 2000; Srivastava et al. 2014, 2015), ETo estimation (Martins et al. 2017; Paredes et al. 2018b, 2021), and representing spatiotemporal variability of surface climate variables (Hua et al. 2019; Simmons et al. 2017; Simmons et al. 2010) over the globe.

Even with their limitations, reanalysis datasets are incredibly valuable. They provide a consistent, long-term, and globally complete picture of the atmosphere—something no network of weather stations can match. Researchers accept that there are biases (systematic errors), but they can often correct for them or use the data in ways that minimize their impact.
The coarse spatial resolution of global reanalysis datasets can be improved by downscaling them into a finer resolution suitable for hydrological and meteorological applications.

Downscaling is like using a zoom lens on a blurry photo. You start with a low-resolution image (the reanalysis data) and use additional information—like detailed terrain maps or local weather patterns—to create a sharper, higher-resolution version. There are different ways to do this, but one powerful method uses *mesoscale models*—weather models that simulate atmospheric processes at regional scales with much finer grids.

Ishak et al. (2010) used the mesoscale modeling system 5 numerical weather model (MM5) to downscale the ECMWF ERA-40 reanalysis data into finer resolutions in space and time in Brue catchment, southwestern England, showing that downscaling generally improves the quality of reanalysis data.

MM5 is a sophisticated computer model that simulates how air moves, heats up, and interacts with the land surface. By feeding it the coarse ERA-40 data as a starting point, and then letting it run over a small region (the Brue catchment) with a high-resolution grid, the model can generate more realistic weather patterns—like how wind flows around hills or how temperature changes across a valley.

Srivastava et al. (2013) used the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) mesoscale model for downscaling ECMWF ERA-interim and NCEP reanalysis datasets for the same study area and observed a much better performance for downscaled ECMWF than the NCEP.

WRF is another advanced weather model, widely used in research. The fact that ECMWF data performed better than NCEP after downscaling suggests that the quality of the *input* reanalysis matters—even after refinement, a poor starting point limits the final result. ECMWF products are generally considered more accurate due to their advanced data assimilation techniques.

Srivastava et al. (2014) also used the WRF coupled with the NOAH Land Surface Model for downscaling hydro-meteorological variables from the ECMWF dataset for rainfall-runoff modeling in the same study area and found the ECMWF ETo comparable to that computed with observation data.

This is a strong validation. It means that after downscaling, the estimated ETo from reanalysis was almost as good as what you’d get from actual weather station measurements. That’s impressive—and it shows that with the right tools, reanalysis data can be made useful even for local water resource studies.

Similarly, Boulard et al. (2016) used ERA-Interim reanalysis data for a regional analysis of ETo at daily to interannual time scales and found the variables used for ETo and water balance computations are reasonably accurate.
This reinforces the idea that reanalysis, while not perfect, captures the essential dynamics of the climate system well enough for many practical applications.

More recently, Paredes et al. (2018b) evaluated the quality of ERA-Interim reanalysis products for computing PM-ETo across mainland Portugal and found high correlations between the reanalysis and observed temperature variables, particularly when corrections are made for altitudes at grid points.

This highlights a recurring theme: elevation matters. Even in reanalysis, temperature depends strongly on height. If you don’t adjust for the difference between the model’s grid elevation and the actual station elevation, your temperature estimates will be off. But when you apply a simple correction—like adjusting for a lapse rate (the rate at which temperature drops with height)—the match improves dramatically.

They also showed that Rs, the main driving variable of ETo, is accurately estimated by the reanalysis with only a slight overestimation, and the reanalysis wind speed is the least accurate variable examined.

Rs refers to solar radiation—the energy from the sun that powers evaporation. Since ETo is highly sensitive to sunlight, getting Rs right is crucial. The fact that ERA-Interim estimates it well (with just a small overestimation) is excellent news. Wind speed, on the other hand, is harder to capture because it’s influenced by local terrain and surface roughness—factors that coarse models often miss. So it’s no surprise that wind speed is the weakest link.

By combining the NCEP/NCAR re-analysis dataset with observation-based datasets Sheffield et al. (2006) have created a blended dataset that retains the consistency and continuity of the reanalysis constraint to the best available global observation datasets.

This is a smart hybrid approach. Reanalysis gives you continuity and global coverage; observations give you local accuracy. By blending them, you get the best of both worlds—a dataset that’s both complete and realistic. The blending process likely involves adjusting the reanalysis values to match observed trends or averages in regions where good data exist.
The blended datasets hereafter called the NCEP/NCAR-PrincUV have been already used to study spatial variation and temporal trends of drought over the globe (Sheffield et al. 2012).

Drought monitoring requires long, consistent records of water availability—exactly what this blended dataset provides. By feeding it into hydrological models, researchers can track how droughts develop, how severe they are, and how they’re changing over time.

More recently, Martins et al. (2017) have assessed the performance of the climate variables of NCEP/NCAR-PrincUV over the Iberian Peninsula and found them very suitable for ETo estimation. They concluded that the good correspondence between PM-ETo computed with the NCEP/NCAR-PrincUV and the observed climate variables at weather stations is because of the good match between solar radiation and maximum temperature derived from reanalysis and in situ observations.

This is a key finding: the blended dataset works well in Iberia because the solar radiation and temperature values align closely with what’s actually measured on the ground. These two variables are the biggest drivers of ETo, so when they’re accurate, the overall ETo estimate tends to be reliable.

The good results obtained by Martins et al. (2017) can be related to the fact that the Iberian Peninsula shares a relatively dense network of stations with the gridded datasets used by Sheffield et al. (2006) to construct the NCEP/NCAR-PrincUV products.

This is a crucial point. The blending process relies on real observations to correct the reanalysis. If there are many stations in a region, the corrections are more robust. But if there are very few stations, the dataset has little to "learn" from, and the reanalysis errors may remain uncorrected.
